impartial

/im-PAR-shul/ — rhymes with marshal · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is impartial does not favor one side over another, instead making judgments based on facts rather than personal feelings.

An impartial jury listens to both sides before deciding.

Example

When judging the art competition, the teacher stayed impartial, evaluating each piece on technique and creativity and setting aside her personal taste in art so every student had a fair chance.

Impartial is more precise than 'fair' because it specifically describes judging based on facts and merit rather than personal feelings or bias. It emphasizes the method—facts, not feelings—not just the outcome of equal treatment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fair: Fair is the broadest word for treating people rightly and equally, and it describes the outcome — everyone got a fair share, a fair chance. Impartial is narrower and points at the judge: it means having no favorite side at all, so the decision rests on the facts alone.

evenhanded: Evenhanded means dealing out equal treatment — giving both sides the same time, the same rules, the same benefit of the doubt. Impartial reaches one step further back, to the judge's own mind: an impartial judge has no leaning that needs correcting, and decides purely on the facts.

just: Just means morally right — it measures a decision against moral standards, as in a just law or a just punishment. Impartial measures the decision-maker instead: an impartial referee favors neither side, whatever the moral stakes. A ruling can be reached impartially and still turn out to be unjust.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

biased: unfairly favoring one side over another

prejudiced: judging beforehand without fair evidence

Where it sits · how free of bias the judgment

prejudiced → opinionated → objective → impartial

prejudiced vs. impartial: Prejudiced is the extreme opposite of impartial: a prejudiced judge decides before hearing the facts, while an impartial one weighs only the evidence.

opinionated vs. impartial: Opinionated leans much closer to the biased end than impartial does — an opinionated person lets strong personal views color every judgment, which is exactly what an impartial person refuses to do.

objective vs. impartial: Objective is nearly as strong as impartial: both mean sticking to the facts, but impartial adds the specific promise of favoring neither side even when you care about the outcome.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before p) (Latin)

Root — part: a part, share, side (Latin (pars, partis))

Suffix — -ial: relating to (Latin (-alis))

Put it together: im- ('not') + part ('a part, a side') + -ial ('relating to') builds 'not taking a side.' An impartial judge refuses to belong to one 'part' of a dispute and rules on the facts instead — fair even when she has feelings about the outcome.

Use the root in a new word: partial: Grandpa is partial to blueberry pie, and he will drive an hour for a good slice of it.

Word Choice

formal

Reach for impartial when describing judges, juries, or anyone making an important judgment where facts and merit matter more than personal feelings or loyalty. It's stronger and more specific than 'fair,' which just means treating people equally. Impartial emphasizes the method: judging by facts, not bias.
